---
title: "Bayesian Linear Regression"
description: "Original mathematical teaching with a worked delivery-operations example; MML §9.3."
---

**Study reference:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning*, §9.3. The examples, reasoning and notation explanations are written independently.

## Start from a problem

Six delivery observations are too few to pretend model coefficients are known exactly. Bayesian regression represents uncertainty over beta and produces predictive uncertainty for a future order.

## Formulate the problem mathematically

$$
p(\beta\mid\boldsymbol y,X)\propto p(\boldsymbol y\mid X,\beta)p(\beta),\quad p(y_*\mid x_*,\mathcal D)=\int p(y_*\mid x_*,\beta)p(\beta\mid\mathcal D)\,d\beta
$$

This relation identifies the required structure. Interpret the symbols using the stated model rather than memorising the formula without its assumptions.

## Derive a worked result

Assume independent Gaussian observation noise with variance sigma² and a Gaussian prior beta~N(m0,S0). The posterior precision is S0^-1 + X^T X/sigma². A strongly regularising prior suppresses extreme slope estimates when features are weakly identified.

## Why the mathematics matters

The posterior predictive variance combines uncertainty in the learned coefficients with observation noise. A narrower prior is not evidence of more data; it encodes a stronger assumption.

## Explain or calculate

Which part of the predictive distribution would remain uncertain even if beta were known exactly?
